definition: New coal pipeline technologies aim to reduce the water used in slurry transport, but introduce a new cost: the coal must be dried before use, and drying by burning some of the coal raises both emissions and transport cost.
core_idea: Compressed 'coal log' pipelines cut water use dramatically versus slurry pipelines and leave residual water cleaner, but they shift the problem from water consumption to a drying step that itself burns fuel and adds emissions and cost.
key_points: Compressed coal-log pipelines can move three to four tons of coal per ton of water used, versus traditional slurry pipelines.
Coal-log pipelines leave the water cleaner than slurry pipelines do.
Transported coal must be dried before it can be burned as fuel.
Burning some of the coal is the most effective way to dry it, which increases carbon emissions and transportation cost.
relationships: Trade-off between water-use efficiency and drying-related emissions/cost.
trading_implications: Physical logistics costs (drying, transport) are a real cost layer that affects delivered coal economics, distinct from mine-mouth price.
caveats: Reducing water usage in coal transport is not a free efficiency gain; it trades one input cost/environmental cost (water) for another (drying emissions and expense).
